extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and theatre/dance practitioners (poets, critics, actors, dancing-masters, educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and aesthetic principles for composing and judging sublime epic poetry (illustrated by commentary on Milton's Sixth Book of Paradise Lost), with additional evaluative remarks on dancing and theatrical performance. Contains examples, comparisons to classical models, and practical suggestions for pacing and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity / grandeur of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should raise his imagination above itself when treating great subjects; the Battle of Angels is always spoken of in images of greatness and terror suitable to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's descriptions (e.g., burning darts, thunders, tearing up mountains, Messiah's pomp) exemplify how sublime imagery should astonish the reader. Quotations from Milton are used to show the effect. The passage stresses that every mention of this battle is in exalted terms appropriate to omnipotence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the mean or trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: An exactness of judgment is required to avoid everything that might appear light or trivial in descriptions of great subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Homer/Claudian puerilities (e.g., comic images of throwing islands or rivers flowing down a giant's back) which verge on burlesque. The critic praises Milton for retaining grandeur without descending into ludicrous extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between bold invention and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold imaginative inventions (such as assigning artillery to rebel angels) may be permissible if they are appropriate to the characters and the internal logic of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay defends Milton's bold thought of rebel angels using artillery as fitting for beings aspiring to imitate divine thunder; justify daring imagery by its consonance with the subject's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and improvement of classical and scriptural models
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should draw upon the sublime hints of ancient poets and sacred scripture, taking what is great and avoiding what is puerile, and improve upon those hints in service of his subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Milton borrows grandeur from Homer (battles rising in scale), Claudian (wild inventions used selectively), Virgil (divine weapons), and Ezekiel / Psalms (Messiah's chariot imagery). The critic commends Milton for compositing these helps into a superior depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive escalation of scene and terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Battles (or great scenes) should rise one above another, improving in horror and grandeur toward a climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer's Iliad is cited for how engagements escalate; Milton's Fight of Angels similarly progresses from fire-dart volleys to artificial thunders to the tearing up of mountains and finally the Messiah's coming—each stage increases the scale and awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale and choice of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Images employed must fit the scale of the subject (e.g., omnipotence invites images of thunder, earthquakes, mountains) and not introduce incongruous or petty details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes Milton's consistent selection of large, terrible images (shouts of armies, brazen chariots, hurling of rocks) and praises how these give readers a suitable idea of so great an action; small or incongruous details would diminish the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of burlesque and puerility
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when employing extravagant imagery, the poet must avoid images that tend toward burlesque or ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claudian's and other ancient poets' more wanton inventions (islands whirled to the skies, rivers flowing down a giant's back) are given as anti-examples; Milton achieves the sublime without such laughable excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and provision of 'resting-places' for the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When sustaining great imaginative exertions, the poem should intersperse speeches, reflections, similitudes and other reliefs to diversify narration and ease the reader's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton is praised for interspersing such reliefs so readers may recover and be refreshed before the next great action; this contrast intensifies the effect of the nobler parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegorical or symbolic bestowals to signify favor
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowing a favored hero with an allegorical weapon or token from a deity is an established poetic device to convey divine favor and elevate the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Michael's sword from God's armory (parallel to Virgil's Æneas receiving a sword), and biblical precedents (Maccabees), used as a legitimate, venerable convention to impart moral/divine legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveying majesty by restraint (implying more than described)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may intentionally withhold the full exercise of a character's power so that the reader conceives an idea beyond what is directly described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's Messiah 'puts not forth half his strength, but checks his thunder in mid volley; for he meant Not to destroy, but root them out of Heaven'—restraint implies greater majesty than overt display could.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing as formative art for deportment and public carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing is an art that improves a person's mien, gesture, motion, and aspect; it refines deportment even for those naturally graceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that small attainments like dancing materially affect how people present themselves in assemblies; a 'good Mein' arises from practice guided by reason as well as nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for fundamental rules and instruction in dancing
rubrics_metrics.description: To restore and improve dancing, it is necessary to set down fundamental rules and cultivate its practice, both to better enable performers and to educate spectators in judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author (a dancing-master) proposes an essay/treatise covering antiquity, nature and perfection of parts, particular dances, and the origin/progress of dance notation so masters and audiences may be improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive physicality in acting (movement as characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical movement and carriage (the step, the manner of marching to a throne) should express majestic or great conceptions and contribute to a character's effect on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Booth's march as Pyrrhus convinces the critic that majestic conceptions are expressed in the very step; dancing training would further enhance such stage expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of speech and intelligibility in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragic performance, actors' speech should be such that the audience understands their meaning; intelligibility is a consideration in dramatic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Roger's remark—'Should your People in Tragedy always talk to be understood?'—raises the issue whether tragic diction should prioritize comprehension; the anecdote suggests the critic values clarity alongside other dramatic rules.
